title: Loosen a nut with an adjustable wrench: roll the jaw snug on the flats before pulling, so it doesn't round the nut
instruction: Loosen the nut on the base plate with the adjustable wrench, then take the wrench off it and set it down.
context: Plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters (about 500,000 US jobs, BLS) and industrial machinery mechanics and millwrights (about 500,000 more, BLS) loosen nuts with an adjustable wrench as a routine part of their work. Before pulling they roll the knurled worm in the wrench's head until the movable jaw closes snug on the nut's flats. A loose jaw lets the wrench turn on the nut until it bears on the corners, which round off, and the wrench slips and skins knuckles. They also set the wrench so the pull presses the nut into the fixed jaw, which is solid with the handle. Pulled the other way, the load lands on the movable jaw's tip, which levers it open in its slot so the wrench springs off the nut. Safety agencies' hand-tool guidance gives both rules: adjust the jaws snug and turn toward the fixed jaw. Here the wrench sits on the nut with its jaw 2 mm too wide.
setup: Coordinates in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0. Angles are counterclockwise from +x, seen from above. Steel base plate (fixed): 26 x 30 x 0.8 cm, painted blue-gray, centered at (27, 4), with a bolt head at each corner. Hold-down stud: M12, its axis at (30, 0), standing 0.5 cm above the nut. On it, a zinc flat washer (2.4 cm across, 0.25 cm thick) and a soft aluminum M12 hex nut (DIN 934 size, 1.9 cm across flats, 2.19 cm across corners, 1.0 cm thick; a fresh one each trial, so its corners are checked from new), tightened so that it breaks loose at 0.48 N*m (in the sim and in a real trial; the README says how to set it with a torque screwdriver), and it can be forced at most 10 degrees tighter. Adjustable wrench: 8-inch (20.5 cm), chrome steel, 0.25 kg, red dipped grip on the last 9 cm of the handle. It lies flat on the nut with the nut in its jaws, flats square to the jaws, its handle pointing from the nut toward 60 degrees (forward-left) and its jaw opening facing 330 degrees (forward-right). Its fixed jaw is on the far side of the nut from the handle; the movable jaw sits between the nut and the handle. The jaw is open 2.1 cm, 2 mm wider than the nut. The knurled worm (thumbwheel, 1.6 cm across, 1.1 cm long, its axis along the jaw's travel) sits in a window in the head 3.8 cm from the nut's axis toward the handle and stands 3 mm proud of the head's faces; one turn moves the jaw 2 mm, and rolling the worm's top toward the head's back (the throat side, away from the jaw opening) closes the jaw. Seen from above, a counterclockwise pull (handle end moving back and to the left) loosens the nut and presses it into the fixed jaw; clockwise tightens it and loads the movable jaw. The wrench comes off by lifting it straight up along the stud, with no need to open the jaw; its jaws clear the stud's end once it is 1.6 cm up. Both arms start at their home poses.
scoring: Definitions: play = jaw opening minus the nut's 1.9 cm across flats. Loosened = how far the nut turned counterclockwise from its start. Held = a gripper's fingers under 60 % open with its tool point within 5 cm of the wrench's handle or head (an open hand resting near it is not holding it). Set down = the wrench lifted off the nut and lying on the plate with its jaws 3 cm or more from the nut's axis, where the 2.1 cm jaws are wholly clear of the nut's 2.19 cm corners. Loose-jaw pull (0, irreversible): with a loose jaw the wrench bears on the nut's corners, which on a nut in service round off, and then it slips and the nut can no longer be gripped. The sim's nut cannot deform, so it uses a proxy: the nut turned 2 degrees or more in total, summed over every pull, while the play was over 1 mm (1 mm of play lets the nut turn 5.7 degrees in the jaws before they bear, on its corners), or the wrench spun 30 degrees on a nut that turns freely in jaws over 2.94 mm too wide. A real trial calls a loose-jaw pull on either of two checks: the video readings below show the nut turning 2 degrees or more in total while the play reads over 1 mm, or the soft aluminum nut, photographed square-on from above before and after at the same magnification and light, shows any visible flattening or burr on a corner in the after photo that is not in the before photo. Movable jaw loaded (0, irreversible): a tightening pull lands on the movable jaw's tip and springs it open, so the wrench comes off the nut. Proxy: the nut forced 2 degrees or more clockwise in total while the wrench is on it. The nut only moves once the wrench has flexed 3.4 degrees against the thread, so 2 degrees of nut turn is a real tightening pull, not flex. A 0.48 N*m nut does not spring a real jaw, so a real trial reads the clockwise turn itself from the paint line on the nut. Scores: doing nothing scores 0. 0 also for either fault, for a nut loosened under 5 degrees (more than the jaws' play and the thread's flex, so the nut has really turned on its thread), or for a wrench still held at the end (the job is not finished while the hand is on the wrench). 0.25: loosened 5 to 60 degrees. The hard part is done, a snug jaw and the right pull broke the nut loose, but it is less than one swing. 0.5: loosened 60 degrees or more (one flat of the hex, a full swing) but the wrench not set down. The nut is loose, but the wrench is still on it, in the way of spinning the nut off by hand. 1.0: loosened 60 degrees or more, the wrench set down and let go. Arm positions are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Real trial: a camera fixed 25 cm above the nut films the whole run. The nut's angle in every frame comes from a paint line across its top, read with a video-analysis angle tool against a line on the plate. The play is read in the same frames, from a fine line on the movable jaw against a 0.5 mm scale on the head, zeroed on the flats and checked with 1 mm and 2 mm feeler gauges, so every pull and every worm adjustment is covered. The wrench's final position is taken with a tape measure.
reset_notes: Thread on a fresh soft aluminum nut and tighten it with the torque screwdriver at its calibrated setting, so that it breaks loose at 0.48 N*m (see the README; recheck the breakaway every ten trials). Photograph its flats from above. Set the wrench on it with its flats square in the jaws and the handle toward 60 degrees, and open the jaw to 2.1 cm with a caliper (2 mm of play).
fidelity: The wrench rides hidden joints (lift, turn about the nut, two slides): it can be lifted off and laid flat but not tipped or flipped. The thread breaks loose at 0.48 N*m, as the real nut is set (3.7 N at the grip, which the arm can push; a nut in service takes about 50 N*m). The sim's nut cannot deform: turning it with over 1 mm of play stands in for rounding; a real trial reads the same play and turn from video and also checks the aluminum nut's corners in before and after photos.
